Solution

Words: 128
2I OurBigBook.com
Chebyshev's equal-ripple criterion says that a polynomial q of degree at most m is a best uniform approximation to a continuous function F if and only if the error F−q attains alternating extrema of maximum magnitude at m+2 ordered points.
Since Tn​ has leading coefficient 2n−1, the polynomial 21−nTn​ is monic and alternates between ±21−n at tj​=cos(jπ/n). Therefore
q∗​(t)=tn−21−nTn​(t),degq<nmin​∥tn−q∥∞​=21−n.​
(6)
At each tj​, both Tn​−f and Tn​+f have sign (−1)j, because ∣f(tj​)∣<1. Each has a root in every interval between consecutive extrema, hence all its at most n roots lie in (−1,1). For t>1 both polynomials remain positive, giving ∣f(t)∣<Tn​(t). For t<−1 both have sign (−1)n, giving ∣f(t)∣<∣Tn​(t)∣. On [−1,1] the hypothesis gives ∣f∣<1. Thus
∣f(t)∣<max{1,∣Tn​(t)∣}(t∈R).​
(7)
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

3K (Coding & Cryptography)

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 103
3K OurBigBook.com
The received word 001 has Hamming distances 1 from 000 and 2 from 111, so
P(001∣000)=649​,P(001∣111)=643​.
(8)
After multiplying by the priors, the unnormalized posterior probabilities are 9/320 and 12/320. Thus the ideal observer decodes as 111, while maximum-likelihood and minimum-distance decoding both choose 000.
The ideal observer minimizes average error but needs priors and channel statistics. Maximum likelihood needs the channel law but not priors, and can be suboptimal for unequal codeword probabilities. Minimum distance is simple and agrees with maximum likelihood for a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability below 1/2, but ignores unequal priors and general channel asymmetry.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

a OurBigBook.com
A language L satisfies the context-free pumping lemma if there is an integer p≥1 such that every z∈L with ∣z∣≥p has a decomposition
z=uvwxy
(9)
with
∣vwx∣≤p,∣vx∣≥1,
(10)
and
uviwxiy∈Lfor every i≥0.
(11)
Every context-free language has this property, although the property by itself is not sufficient for context-freeness.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Words: 309 Articles: 8

i

Words: 97 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
i OurBigBook.com
This language is not context-free. If p were a pumping length, apply the lemma to
z=0p1p0p.
(12)
Because ∣vwx∣≤p, the pumped region meets at most two adjacent blocks and cannot meet both zero blocks. Pumping with i=0 or i=2 changes at least one symbol count. If it changes either zero block, that block no longer agrees with the untouched zero block; if it changes only the middle block, the number of ones no longer agrees with the two zero counts. In every case the pumped word leaves the language, contradicting the lemma.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

ii OurBigBook.com

S⟶0S0∣1S1∣00∣11.
(13)
Every derivation adds matching symbols to the two ends and starts with a matching central pair, so it produces exactly the nonempty even palindromes wwR.

iii

Words: 122 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 122
iii OurBigBook.com
This language is not context-free. Intersect it with the regular language
R=0+1+0+.
(14)
An even palindrome in R has the form 0r12s0r, and its first half is w=0r1s. The required equality of the numbers of zeros and ones in w forces r=s. Hence the intersection is
L∩R={0n12n0n:n>0}.
(15)
This is not context-free: applying the pumping lemma to 0p12p0p, a pumped substring of length at most p cannot meet both zero blocks. Pumping therefore either destroys equality of the two zero counts or changes the middle count away from twice their common value.
Context-free languages are closed under intersection with regular languages, so a context-free L would make L∩R context-free. This contradiction proves the claim.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Write Ygj​ for the yield in replicate j of genotype g∈{aa,Aa,AA}. Model 1 is the one-way cell-means model
Ygj​=μg​+εgj​,εgj​∼iidN(0,σ2).
(18)
Thus its three coefficients estimate the three genotype means directly.
Put Di​=1{counti​≥1}. Model 2 is
Yi​=β0​+β1​Di​+εi​,εi​∼iidN(0,σ2).
(19)
It imposes μAa​=μAA​=β0​+β1​ and μaa​=β0​. The reported finite-sample p-values assume independent normal errors, a common unknown variance in every genotype, fixed full-rank design matrices, and correctness of the relevant mean model. Random assignment of genotypes supports interpreting the fitted differences as treatment effects.

The displayed analysis of variance compares Model 2 with the unrestricted three-mean Model 1. It tests
H0​:μAa​=μAA​,
(20)
which is precisely full dominance: once an A allele is present, a second copy has no further effect. Under H0​,
F=48.487/57(54.148−48.487)/1​=6.6551∼F1,57​.
(21)
The p-value 0.01249 rejects full dominance at the 5% level, providing evidence that the heterozygote and AA means differ.

a OurBigBook.com
The term −IS removes healthy foxes through mass-action contact with infectives. The Laplacian ∇2I models random migration of infected foxes. The matching term +IS creates newly infected animals, while −μI removes infectives at per-capita rate μ. The equation Rt​=μI records those removed from infectious circulation, for example foxes that have died from rabies; they neither migrate nor return to susceptibility in this model.

In a homogeneous population,
I˙=(S−μ)I.
(23)
An infected fox remains infectious for mean time 1/μ and creates new infections at initial rate S0​, so the basic reproductive ratio is
R0​=μS0​​.​
(24)
Initially I grows exactly when S0​−μ>0, equivalently R0​>1. Below that threshold each infective produces fewer than one replacement on average and the infection decays.

The residues at i and −i are respectively 1/(2i) and −1/(2i). If two paths from 0 to z have winding-number differences n+​ and n−​ about those poles, their integrals differ by
2πi(2in+​​−2in−​​)=π(n+​−n−​).
(33)
Loops can wind around either pole independently, so the value changes by arbitrary integer multiples of π and F is multivalued.
Along the straight real segment,

Let Γ be any closed curve in C∖B. Since the arc B joins −i to i without meeting Γ, those two points lie in the same component of C∖Γ. Their winding numbers about Γ are therefore equal. The residue theorem gives
∮Γ​1+t2dt​=π{wind(Γ,i)−wind(Γ,−i)}=0.
(36)
Thus every closed-path period vanishes. Integrals from 0 to z along any two paths avoiding B agree, so FB​ is single-valued. Notice that this argument uses cancellation of the two residues; simple connectedness of the slit domain is not required.

FB​(z)=2π​+O(∣z∣−1).

a OurBigBook.com
For a one-dimensional closed energy orbit, define
I(E)=2π1​∮p(q,E)dq.
(41)
After locally inverting this relation to write E=H(I), use the Hamilton--Jacobi generating function
W(q,I)=∫qp(q′,I)dq′
(42)
and define the angle ϕ=∂W/∂I modulo 2π. The transformation is canonical, the Hamiltonian depends only on I, and
I˙=0,ϕ˙​=dIdH​=ω(I).
(43)
The adiabatic-invariance principle says that if an external parameter changes on a time scale much longer than the orbital period, and no separatrix is crossed, the action I remains approximately constant. Its small within-cycle changes do not accumulate at leading adiabatic order.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Put ϵ=∣E∣>0. On the energy surface,
2mp2​=∣q∣1​−ϵ≥0,
(44)
so
∣q∣≤qmax​=ϵ1​.​
(45)
Equality occurs at a turning point, so this is the smallest possible bound.
Using the natural collision continuation through the singular point, a full orbit runs between both turning points. Hence
I=2π1​∮pdq=π2​∫01/ϵ​2m(q1​−ϵ)​dq.
(46)
Set q=x2/ϵ. Then
∫01/ϵ​2m(q1​−ϵ)​dq=2ϵ2m​​∫01​1−x2​dx=2π​ϵ2m​​.
(47)
Therefore
I=∣E∣2m​​.​
(48)
If instead one identifies the singularity as a reflecting endpoint and regards one half-line as the orbit, the action is half this value; the following scaling is identical.
Adiabatic invariance keeps m/∣E∣ constant. Thus doubling m doubles ∣E∣:
∣E∣final​=2∣E∣initial​,Efinal​=2Einitial​.​
(49)
The energy becomes twice as negative.

ni​≃gi​(2πℏ2mi​kB​T​)3/2exp(kB​Tμi​−mi​c2​).

Neutrons and protons have equal spin degeneracy and nearly equal masses, so their prefactor ratio is approximately one. Hence
np​nn​​≃exp[−kB​T(mn​−mp​)c2​]=e−Q/(kB​T).​

The compactness theorem states that a set T of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of T has a model.
The forward implication follows by using the same model for every finite subset. Conversely, suppose every finite subset of T has a model. If T were inconsistent, a formal derivation of ⊥ from T would use only finitely many assumptions, say those in T0​⊆T. Then T0​ would be inconsistent. By part (b), T0​ would have no model, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus T is consistent, and part (b) gives a model of T.

A matching from X to Y is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges that covers every vertex of X. Equivalently, it chooses for each x∈X a distinct neighbour in Y.
Hall marriage theorem says that such a matching exists if and only if
∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣for every S⊆X.
(154)
Necessity is immediate: the distinct partners of the vertices in S all belong to N(S).
For sufficiency, induct on ∣X∣. The claim is clear when ∣X∣=1. First suppose every nonempty proper S⊂X satisfies the strict inequality ∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣+1. Choose an edge xy and delete x and y. For S⊆X∖{x}, deletion removes at most one neighbour, so
∣NG−{x,y}​(S)∣≥∣NG​(S)∣−1≥∣S∣.
(155)
Induction gives a matching of X∖{x}, and adding xy completes it.
Otherwise there is a nonempty proper S⊂X with ∣N(S)∣=∣S∣. Hall's condition holds in the bipartite graph induced by S∪N(S), so induction matches S onto N(S). For A⊆X∖S,
∣N(A∪S)∣≥∣A∣+∣S∣,
(156)
and hence A has at least ∣A∣ neighbours outside N(S). Induction therefore matches X∖S into Y∖N(S). The two matchings are disjoint and together cover X.

Solution

Words: 250
24G OurBigBook.com
The identity theorem says that if two holomorphic functions on a connected Riemann surface agree on a set having an accumulation point, then they agree everywhere.
Apply local coordinates to their difference F. The power-series proof in the plane shows that near any point, either F vanishes identically or its zeros are isolated: if the first nonzero Taylor coefficient has order m, then F(z)=(z−z0​)mG(z) with G(z0​)=0. An accumulation point of the zero set therefore has a neighbourhood on which F=0. The set of points having such a neighbourhood is nonempty and open. It is also closed: near a limit point, a coordinate neighbourhood contains an open set on which F=0, and the planar identity theorem makes F vanish throughout that coordinate neighbourhood. Connectedness now makes this set the whole surface.
For a nonempty connected open set U⊂R2, a function h:U→R is harmonic when h∈C2(U) and
Δh=hxx​+hyy​=0.
(234)
On a sufficiently small disc, the one-form
−hy​dx+hx​dy
(235)
is closed and hence equals dk for some k. The Cauchy--Riemann equations then make h+ik holomorphic. Holomorphic functions are smooth, so h∈C∞(U).
A real-valued function H on a Riemann surface is harmonic when, in every holomorphic chart z, its coordinate expression is harmonic. This definition is chart-independent. If w=w(z) is a holomorphic transition map, the chain rule and Cauchy--Riemann equations give
Δz​(H∘w)=∣w′(z)∣2(Δw​H)∘w.
(236)
Thus vanishing of the Laplacian is preserved by every change of holomorphic coordinate.

The jump chain moves away from zero with probability 2/3 and towards zero with probability 1/3 on either half-line. Starting from 1, the probability that this biased walk ever hits zero is (1/3)/(2/3)=1/2, and the same holds starting from −1. Thus the return probability to zero is 1/2<1. The jump chain, and hence X, is transient.
It is also explosive. The transient jump chain visits zero only finitely often. After its last visit it stays on one half-line, and the strong law for its increments gives
n∣Yn​∣​⟶31​
(282)
almost surely. In particular, eventually ∣Yn​∣≥n/6. Conditional on the jump-chain path, the mean total remaining holding time is
∑n​qYn​​1​=∑n​3−∣Yn​∣<∞.
(283)
The sum of the actual nonnegative holding times is therefore finite almost surely, so infinitely many jumps occur in finite time.
Despite this, the chain has an invariant distribution in the continuous-time balance-equation sense πQ=0. Detailed balance across the edge from zero to one gives π1​=π0​/2, and on each half-line it gives
πi​πi+1​​=qi+1,i​qi,i+1​​=32​.
(284)
By symmetry and normalization,
π0​=41​,πi​=π−i​=81​(32​)i−1quad(i≥1).​
(285)
This example also shows why, for an explosive chain, existence of an invariant distribution need not imply positive recurrence.

{Fi​,Fj​}=0for all i,j.

ω=∑i=1n​dIi​∧dθi​,H=H(I),

and Hamilton's equations become
I˙i​=0,θ˙i​=∂Ii​∂H​.

Rαγ​=Rμαμγ​.

Rαγ​−Rγα​=0,

so the Ricci tensor is symmetric.

At zero Reynolds number, an incompressible Newtonian fluid obeys the Stokes equations
−∇p+μ∇2u=0,∇⋅u=0.
(437)
Taking the divergence gives ∇2p=0. Taking the curl and writing ω=∇×u gives
μ∇2ω=0.
(438)
Thus both pressure and vorticity are harmonic in the fluid.
In the laboratory frame, the boundary conditions are
u→0(r→∞),
(439)
and, on r=a,
u⋅n=U⋅n,(I−nnT)u=(I−nnT)U.
(440)
The first is impermeability of the solid surface and the second is viscous no slip. Together they say u=U on the sphere.
For the stated solution, put
A(r)=4r3a​+4r3a3​,B(r)=4r33a​−4r53a3​,s=U⋅x.

All wavevectors lie in the xz plane. The incident P-wave travels upward toward the interface. In the lower medium there are a reflected P-wave, polarized parallel to its reflected wavevector, and a reflected SV-wave, polarized in the xz plane perpendicular to its wavevector. In the upper medium there are transmitted P and SV waves with the corresponding longitudinal and transverse polarizations. No SH wave is generated by this in-plane incident field.
Frequency and tangential phase matching give Snell's law: every wave has the same ω and the same tangential wavenumber kx​, while its normal wavenumber has the sign appropriate to reflection or transmission.
For a perfectly bonded interface, displacement and traction are continuous:
[ux​]=[uz​]=0,[σxz​]=[σzz​]=0
(466)
in the two-dimensional problem. In three dimensions one also includes [uy​]=[σyz​]=0. Here
σij​=λ(∇⋅u)δij​+μ(∂i​uj​+∂j​ui​).
(467)
These four in-plane conditions determine the four reflected and transmitted amplitudes.

The assumption of no evanescence requires sinϕ≤1/2.
With a common suppressed factor e−iωt, take
uI​uR​uT​​=(sinϕ,0,cosϕ)eik(xsinϕ+zcosϕ),=R(sinϕ,0,−cosϕ)eik(xsinϕ−zcosϕ),=T(sinψ,0,cosψ)eik^(xsinψ+zcosψ).​

For an inviscid liquid, continuity of normal displacement and normal stress gives
cosϕ(1−R)=Tcosψ,Z(1+R)=Z^T,

where Z=λ/cP​ and Z^=λ^/c^P​. Solving,
R=Z^cosϕ+ZcosψZ^cosϕ−Zcosψ​,T=Z^cosϕ+Zcosψ2Zcosϕ​.​

∣Z^cosϕ−Zcosψ∣=2Zcosϕ.

Zcosψ=(Z^−2Z)cosϕ.

sin2ϕ=Z^(Z^−4Z)3Z2−4ZZ^+Z^2​.​

Put ω2N​=e−πi/N and split the transform into its even and odd input samples. If Ek​ and Ok​ are the two length-N transforms, then
Yk​=Ek​+ω2Nk​Ok​,Yk+N​=Ek​−ω2Nk​Ok​,0≤k<N.
(475)
Thus a length-2N transform requires two length-N transforms and O(N) further multiplications. Its multiplication count satisfies
M(2N)≤2M(N)+CN.
(476)
Since N is a power of two, iteration through log2​(2N) levels gives M(2N)=O(NlogN).
